mainEntity.name: Why did my neighbor's fence survive the storm when mine didn't?

acceptedAnswer.text: Almost always post depth and fastener choice. A fence with posts set 42 inches or deeper in sound concrete, with rails screwed or bolted rather than toe-nailed, resists a 70 mph gust that will flatten a fence on 24-inch posts with nailed rails. Age matters less than most people think. A well-built ten-year-old fence routinely outlasts a poorly built three-year-old one.

mainEntity.name: How much wind can a wood privacy fence take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A solid 6-foot panel catches about 9 pounds per square foot at 60 mph and 16 pounds per square foot at 80 mph — roughly 432 and 768 pounds on an 8-foot bay. A properly built Michigan fence with 42-inch footings and 8-foot bays handles ordinary 40-to-60 mph storms comfortably. Sustained 70-to-80 mph gusts with saturated ground are where design and installation quality separate.

mainEntity.name: How deep should fence posts be in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: At least 42 inches below grade, which is the frost depth set statewide by Michigan Residential Code R403.1.4.1. We set 48 inches on gate posts and in low-draining yards. Measured frost penetration in southeast Michigan is usually 30 to 36 inches, so 42 inches carries margin — and a fence post, unlike a house footing, has no dead load holding it down.

mainEntity.name: Does a solid privacy fence blow down more easily than an open one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A solid board-to-board fence presents the maximum sail area and takes the full wind load. A picket fence, a lattice top, or a shadowbox style lets air pass and relieves a meaningful share of the pressure. You can keep full privacy and still reduce load by choosing board-on-board or shadowbox and shortening bay spacing to 6 feet.

mainEntity.name: Is board-on-board stronger than solid board-to-board in wind?

acceptedAnswer.text: Board-on-board is generally more wind-tolerant because the overlap between alternating boards allows a small amount of air passage, and because the double-layer construction stiffens the panel. It is not a free pass — it still needs 42-inch footings and close spacing — but on an exposed lot it is the better choice than flat solid panel.

mainEntity.name: How much does wet snow weigh on a fence?

acceptedAnswer.text: Snow ranges from about 5 pounds per cubic foot for dry powder to as much as 50 for wet, firm snow; one inch of water equivalent is 5.2 pounds per square foot. A foot of wet snow on a top rail is a serious concentrated load at the point of maximum leverage. The bigger winter risk in Oakland County is roof shedding dumping onto the fence line all at once.

mainEntity.name: Does homeowners insurance cover fence wind damage in Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually yes, under the other structures coverage — Coverage B — when the damage is sudden and accidental, such as a windstorm or a fallen tree. Rot, termites, and gradual deterioration are typically excluded. Payout depends on your other-structures limit, deductible, any separate wind deductible, and whether the policy pays replacement cost or actual cash value.

mainEntity.name: How much does storm damage fence repair cost in Oakland County?

acceptedAnswer.text: Single-section repairs in Metro Detroit typically run about 250 to 900 dollars depending on material and how many posts are affected. Resetting or replacing posts pushes toward the upper end because breaking out an old concrete footing is real labor. Widespread damage is quoted on site after a full walk of the run.

mainEntity.name: Should I brace my fence before winter?

acceptedAnswer.text: Brace only a post that has already started to lean; bracing a sound fence adds nothing. For a leaning post, a diagonal 2x4 screwed to a stake will hold it through the winter. Do not pour concrete around a broken or rotted post as a winter fix — it locks the failure in and adds demolition cost to the spring repair.

mainEntity.name: What is the frost line in Oakland County, Michigan?

acceptedAnswer.text: 42 inches below finished grade. Michigan sets that depth statewide in the Residential Code at R403.1.4.1, and local municipalities cannot amend it. Measured frost penetration in southeast Michigan typically runs 30 to 36 inches, so the code figure provides margin for a fence post with nothing but soil holding it in place.
